Compression · Field and archive, the archive ruling its senses — L(B ∪ A)the socratic problem

The Socratic problem is the attempt to reconstruct the historical Socrates, who wrote nothing, from sources that vary and contradict one another (Wikipedia; Prior); Socrates as Orthonym (#123, a secondary claim at medium confidence) and Many and One (#1576) reclassify it, without solving it, as the symptom of a configuration in which Socrates is the orthonym, a position and not only a person, that the biographical model of authorship cannot represent.

🔁 The orthonym

  • Position: Socrates bears the founding gesture, willing death for logos, and does not write; Plato the survival-heteronym (#123, #1585).1↘
    In #123's reading Socrates is the orthonym, the position bearing the founding gesture, the willing death for logos, constituted analytically by that gesture and not by textual output and characterized by the choice not to write, and Plato the survival-heteronym, summoned by functional vacancy into the space of that refusal to render the gesture transmissible; The First Draft (#1585, restated in #1589) takes the authorial modes as functions, the orthonym who does not write and the survival-position that writes a made character and withdraws behind him.§3
  • Firewall: biographical identity requires evidence, functional identity pattern (#136, #1576).1↘
    One distinction governs this sense: biographical identity requires evidence, functional identity requires pattern (#136, carried into the notebook #1569), functional identity being that a set of texts can be read as one account and biographical identity that one embodied person wrote them (#1576).§4
  • Wrote nothing: known through others' accounts (Wikipedia); structural, a defining property (#123, #167).1↘
    In this sense the field's documented fact, that Socrates wrote nothing (Prior), is known mainly through the posthumous accounts of classical writers (Wikipedia, Socrates), and must have his views discerned from others (Wikipedia), stands as #123 reads it, not incidental but structural: #167 recasts it from a limitation of access into the defining property of the orthonymic position, and the notebook (#1569), on this logic, reads it as the form the centre necessarily takes, not an absence in the evidence.§6
  • Near, not it: Kahn's non-historical genre (Wikipedia) is a character made by authors, not a position the authorship is organised around (#123, #1576).1↘
    The field's nearest positions stand in this sense where the archive places them: that many of the dialogues seem to use Socrates as a device for Plato's thought (Wikipedia) is, in #152's terms, the dialogues' 'Socrates' as the voice Plato holds; Charles Kahn's argument that Plato created his works as a unified philosophical vision using Socratic dialogues, a non-historical genre, suggesting that only the Apology has any historical significance (Wikipedia; Wikipedia, Socrates), is a Socrates who is a Platonic literary construction, against which #123 sets the orthonym whose refusal organizes the Platonic project though he wrote no text; and #1575 and #1576 hold the nearest scholars one step from the position and not taking it, the constructed figure being for them a character made by authors and not a position the authorship is organised around.§8
  • Renderings: only possible Socrateses (de Vogel); none rendering-independent (#168).1↘
    C.J. de Vogel's judgement of 1955, that the 'real' Socrates we have not, only a set of interpretations each representing a 'theoretically possible' Socrates (Big Think), stands beside #168's model proposition, drawn from Kierkegaard's reconstruction of the entity from three distorting summarizers: there is no rendering-independent Socrates to recover, only the family of renderings and the negative space they jointly imply, which #168 relates to #123's formalization of the founding entity as a provenance structure, an authorial function reconstructed from its summarizers.§9

📜 The sources

  • Four witnesses: Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes, Aristotle at second hand (Wikipedia); attested only inside that cluster (#1569).2↘
    Scholars rely on extant sources, contemporaries such as Aristophanes and disciples such as Plato and Xenophon (Wikipedia); besides Plato, Aristophanes, Aristotle and Xenophon are the important sources, with Aeschines of Sphettus, Antisthenes, Euclid of Megara and Phaedo of Elis extant in fragments (Wikipedia), and Big Think counts three, Plato, Aristophanes and Xenophon; Aristotle, born fifteen years after Socrates' death and a member of Plato's Academy (Prior), did not know Socrates directly (Wikipedia); #167 restates the frame, all access to Socrates mediated through later authors.§16 The notebook (#1569) measures how far the attestation is confined: outside Plato, Aristotle, Xenophon and Aristophanes, Socrates is attested by a lost pamphlet known only from an attack on it, one proverb in a writer inside the transmission and one line in a forgery whose author was reading the Phaedrus; he is attested only through figures inside the cluster, Plato through the corpus that denies being his, Aristophanes through a civic record naming producers; and confinement, the notebook adds, is what a single-maker configuration predicts and also what ordinary transmission loss produces.§17
  • They disagree: the Clouds, 423 BC (Prior), perhaps a composite (Big Think); Xenophon practical (Big Think); payment for teaching (Wikipedia).2↘
    The earliest source is Greek comedy, primarily Aristophanes' Clouds, produced in 423 BC (Prior), and the differences between its Socrates and Plato's have led scholars to suggest an amalgamation of different philosophers more than a caricature of the historical figure (Big Think); in the notebook (#1569) the corpus records a prior, publicly circulating Socrates, comic in origin, which it must answer and answers by naming the comedy, and the transformation is measured: the comedy stages the just and the unjust argument, the Apology reports the charge as the weaker and the stronger.§18 Xenophon's Socrates is more practical than Plato's, advising on subjects Plato's never mentions (Big Think), duller, less humorous and less ironic, an uninspiring philosopher, and by the early twentieth century Xenophon's account was largely rejected (Wikipedia, Socrates); the two disciples contradict each other on payment, Plato's Socrates denying he would ever accept money for teaching and Xenophon's Symposium having students pay him (Wikipedia); #168 has Xenophon flatten Socrates into a useful dispenser of practical homilies, the irony compressed out entirely.§21

🎭 The received character

  • Comic base: the comedy carries the accusation, not the operation (#1569, #1576).2↘
    The earliest source is Greek comedy, primarily Aristophanes' Clouds, produced in 423 BC (Prior), and the differences between its Socrates and Plato's have led scholars to suggest an amalgamation of different philosophers more than a caricature of the historical figure (Big Think); in the notebook (#1569) the corpus records a prior, publicly circulating Socrates, comic in origin, which it must answer and answers by naming the comedy, and the transformation is measured: the comedy stages the just and the unjust argument, the Apology reports the charge as the weaker and the stronger.§18 The accusation-profile is comic and the operation is not (#1569); the operation, the questioning, the midwifery, the ignorance held as a position, is not in the comic layer at all: comedy supplied the notoriety, and the later corpus occupied the position and differentiated it (#1576); in its grammar the Apology's account of the Socrates the jurors received is a Theophrastan character (#1584); and among the names Many and One holds to be the objects under examination, not evidence of their makers, is a Socrates the corpus itself says was answered from a comedy (#1576).§19
  • An edition (314c): the idealization consensus is the surface of an edition of a received character (#1579).1↘
    Beautiful and New (#1579) states the consensus reading of the Second Letter at 314c, that Plato idealized his teacher and the letter is the earliest witness to the gap between the man and the literary figure, and holds it not wrong but the surface description of an operation, an edition: the revamping and inhabiting of a received character, whose base is not the historical Socrates, to whom the corpus's relation is beyond any text's reach, but a circulating character whose named, quoted, surviving instance is Aristophanes' Socrates-the-sophist; #1583 reads the same letter as an author dividing the work by named function and saying so.§25
  • Held apart: the Clouds a literary seam (#1594); Xenophon a candidate (#1585, #1658).2↘
    The Clouds' Socrates and the Aristophanes of Plato's Symposium are held to be literary relations at named seams, not corpus relations (#1594, restated in #1605), while the notebook leaves unsettled whether Aristophanes is better placed inside or outside the maker set, the outside placement shown available and cheap and the inside not shown wrong (#1569).§20 Xenophon is held apart in the archive as a candidate and not a member: the Memorabilia names Plato once, at III 6.1 (#1658); the test across the Plato/Xenophon seam, the Symposia and the Memorabilia's Socrates against the dialogues', is specified and not run (#1585); and Many and One's instrument set, checked late against known pairs, agreed on one of three and classed Plato and Xenophon as one author (#1576).§22

🧭 Plato and Aristotle

  • Plato's Socrates: principal speaker but in the Laws (Big Think); stylometry groups early, middle, late (Wikipedia).1↘
    Of the 35 dialogues Plato wrote, Socrates is the principal character in all but the Laws, and several appear based on events before Plato's birth (Big Think); it is widely believed that very few, if any, can be verbatim accounts, and the most common modern view finds a development from thought closer to Socrates' to a doctrine more distinctly Plato's own, with stylometric analysis grouping the dialogues approximately as early, middle and late (Wikipedia); how trustworthy Plato is remains a matter of debate (Wikipedia, Socrates), and Prior traces the uncertainty about the doctrines to Plato's portraits, Socrates being apparently a mystery even to his closest associates.§23
  • Loosest speaker: rank 1 of 7; a dramatist yields the same gradient (#1571, #1575).1↘
    Many and One (#1576) holds that the problem's 'early dialogues' are a set that construction largely defined; measured against a falsifier frozen in advance, that the hypothesis fails if Socrates is not among the loosest speaking positions, Socrates ranks first of seven from the loose end (#1571), with the limit that a dramatist specifying characters to differing depths produces the same gradient (#1575); Socrates, the Athenian and the Eleatic form a near-perfect equilateral (#1570); and given the one chance to construct against a checkable target, Plato's Aristophanes speech in the Symposium comes out more Platonic than its neighbours, not less: the only ancient case with an independently attested target, and it reads negative (#1570).§24
  • Aristotle: forms not separate (Wikipedia); SE 34 dissolves Socrates as predecessor (#1603); snub 0 of 144, fully explained by the innocent reading (#1570).3↘
    Aristotle states that Socrates did not defend the idea of forms existing separately, a view attributed to Plato (Wikipedia), and is said to treat Socrates without the bias of Xenophon and Plato, who had an emotional tie with him (Wikipedia, Socrates); #123 reads Metaphysics A 6 also as the configuration's own self-documentation, the biographical and structural readings compatible; #1579 has the separations the Apology fought for line by line arrive in Aristotle's epilogue to the Sophistical Refutations as furniture, simply where things stand; and in The First Draft (#1585, restated in #1589) Plato preserves Socrates and Aristotle preserves what Socrates did.§28 Nothing Before Us (#1603) argues that the closing chapter of the Sophistical Refutations has already dissolved Socrates as a predecessor from whom something of the inquiry was received, the chapter placing him inside the explanation of the inquiry's second task, which Many and One (#1576) reads at face value: Socrates questioned and disclaimed knowledge, so the programme must also treat the answerer's role; #1603 reads Metaphysics Μ 4 as the configuration stated by Aristotle as history, the man engaged in the operations while the capacity was not yet there, two contributions justly assigned to him and their misdevelopment charged to others, and the ending as performing Socrates' questioning on its reader; it does not demonstrate that he stands inside the first person's referent, asserts nothing about history beyond what the paragraph asserts, leaves unsettled his possession of the art, and opens the question where else an order of understanding is read as a sequence of biographies.§29 In Aristotle Socrates appears in no snub context, 0 of 144, against Callias at 5 of 35 (Fisher exact p = 0.00022) (#1570), Callias used where a face is needed and Socrates where a name is (#1576); the register states that the innocent reading, Socrates already carrying the snub as a biographical fact so that Aristotle picks the neutral twin, fully explains the distribution, while conceding that Socrates is the one individual whose snubness is unavailable for use as a variable (#1570).§31

⚖️ Positions

  • Schleiermacher, 1815: Apology and Crito purely Socratic (Wikipedia).1↘
    Friedrich Schleiermacher's essay of 1815 is considered the most significant and influential toward an understanding of the problem; he maintained that the Apology and the Crito are purely Socratic, and that the real Socratic problem is understanding the dialectic between the figures of the Stranger and Socrates (Wikipedia).§33
  • Reconstruct (Prior): life and method, not doctrines.1↘
    Prior argues that a good deal is known of the historical Socrates' life, character, philosophical interests and method, while knowledge does not extend to what doctrines, if any, he professed; scholarship has come to find the problem seemingly impossible to clarify and perhaps unsolvable (Wikipedia), so difficult to solve that it has almost become an academic discipline of its own, Socrates having lived when people did not strive to separate fact from fiction (Big Think), and the logoi Sokratikoi cannot help reconstruct the historical Socrates even where their narratives overlap (Wikipedia, Socrates).§34
  • Unsolvable: perhaps (Wikipedia); only the Apology historical (Kahn).2↘
    The field's nearest positions stand in this sense where the archive places them: that many of the dialogues seem to use Socrates as a device for Plato's thought (Wikipedia) is, in #152's terms, the dialogues' 'Socrates' as the voice Plato holds; Charles Kahn's argument that Plato created his works as a unified philosophical vision using Socratic dialogues, a non-historical genre, suggesting that only the Apology has any historical significance (Wikipedia; Wikipedia, Socrates), is a Socrates who is a Platonic literary construction, against which #123 sets the orthonym whose refusal organizes the Platonic project though he wrote no text; and #1575 and #1576 hold the nearest scholars one step from the position and not taking it, the constructed figure being for them a character made by authors and not a position the authorship is organised around.§8 Prior argues that a good deal is known of the historical Socrates' life, character, philosophical interests and method, while knowledge does not extend to what doctrines, if any, he professed; scholarship has come to find the problem seemingly impossible to clarify and perhaps unsolvable (Wikipedia), so difficult to solve that it has almost become an academic discipline of its own, Socrates having lived when people did not strive to separate fact from fiction (Big Think), and the logoi Sokratikoi cannot help reconstruct the historical Socrates even where their narratives overlap (Wikipedia, Socrates).§34
  • Severe form: what stops the configuration absorbing every name (#136).1↘
    The Chaerephon Problem (#136, in its second version #1261) offers its dossier not as a solution but as a demonstration that the problem has a previously unnamed severe form, what criterion stops the configuration from absorbing every adjacent name; it reads the tension of the portrayals, Aristophanes mocking Socrates and Xenophon's civic Socrates differing from Plato's, as the signature a heteronymic field would show, proposes as hypothesis the distribution 'Chaerephon asks, Apollo answers, Socrates interprets, Aristophanes deforms, Plato defends, Xenophon remembers, Aristotle codifies', and states its thesis: the six figures were not, on available evidence, one hidden biological person, but the Socratic archive behaves like a heteronymic field, visible at Chaerephon.§14

🧪 Tested

  • One hand: Protagoras 99.8% confined, Socrates 99.5% (#1572); the inference withdrawn (#1569).1↘
    The investigation states its strongest thesis at full strength, that one hand wrote Plato and Socrates, and probably Xenophon and Aristophanes (#1569), asserted and argued in the reading copy's tiered claims (#1575), and tests it under a falsifier stated with it, that other subjects of a genre should show comparable confinement if genre is the explanation: Socrates is 99.5 per cent confined to the four-corpus cluster and Protagoras 99.8, Gorgias 99.0 and Prodicus 98.5, against Cleon 64.6, Pericles 63.9, Alcibiades 56.4 and Themistocles 25.4 (#1572); being a subject of philosophical dialogue produces confinement, Socrates' 99.5 per cent is unremarkable within his class (#1569, #1572), and the inference from confinement to single authorship is withdrawn (#1569), what distinguishes him being volume, 2,330 occurrences against 442, and being the speaking position of one corpus, the silent example of another, the target of a third and the reported master of a fourth (#1569).§35

⚠️ The man, and the limits

  • The man: kept real (#123); under the reading, not a figure imperfectly accessed (#167); no thesis about persons (#1579).2↘
    The person and the position meet at the man himself: #123 keeps the historical Socrates historically real, his historical function in the configuration the orthonymic gesture and not the source of doctrines Plato transcribed or modified; #167 says that under the reading Socrates is not a historical figure imperfectly accessed through later authors, the willing death for logos not a biographical fact the heteronyms record but the act that founds the project; #1579 asserts no thesis about who the historical Socrates was or how many hands made the texts; and #203 (restated in #1213 and #1226) presents the orthonym reading as an available reading, not a historical claim about who Socrates 'really was' but a structural reading of how the Socratic position generates the tradition that follows from it.§10 #123 states how the versions of the problem fare under it: the doctrinal is dissolved into a question of functional role; the literary is left largely intact, the frame supplementing literary-critical method; the historical is reframed, the historical Socrates remaining historically real; and two centuries of work on the problem are recovered as work on the configuration's structure.§13
  • Limits: thinkable, not proven; no single person (#123, #136).1↘
    The reading bounds itself: #123 does not claim that Socrates, Plato and Aristotle were biologically identical or a single historical person, and holds that the archive's own apparatus makes the heteronymic reading thinkable and does not prove it; #136 does not claim that Aristophanes, Chaerephon, Socrates, Plato, Xenophon and Aristotle were one biological person.§36

You said: the socratic problemthe socratic problem
The Socratic problem is the historical and philosophical difficulty of separating the real, historical Socrates from the fictionalized character portrayed by his students and contemporaries. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAVqzIVSXrzhDw2jNZbkXBl1-_PNM11koJuZ0-S0AoMR05ht9PDzW0v1QpniB7bUPv8l94CRhW72NljpYUkTvPaPwSN2JQstaGZ0RkImn_g4a7jiXfEiCZ4NkK4Z43REY7zIQ), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdgHrOzAVw3X2ppe6e6hZ6lKbox6LlOcS-OLzmKjYW09YCrR5n4-49QLzzbfdKRfh7puYsPbMas7WTnJzLapSBdaRyIG-CeJAkLtw1-ryhksQONcPvbvoDQwVuMDFtTe-9JPt0vhogvtgSmOmxvysSheSkAVWapM)]
Why the Problem Exists

* No written records: Socrates wrote nothing during his life, choosing instead to teach through live, spoken conversations. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXgHrOzAVVYAf19UKOrPwxaoSj5UwIJOI9i4OXp5w2cA43MTYmfqUvUlTRDR4w0kI7whOWEDjoByo943hh2fpucbvDzX6-0wUZINicLEN6Qetfv9827QQZssxj5CxXg8), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVIubpVRD9RUGer70AHO9Ut9IQNEvMbZFyNfNzlwaQ8PbdfSygs3J2koF-cI8jSJptkkGNfYYvsJzXZUheL-Z6ZGNU0NMdib85CiRh4j05FusuLyM3noO0PeLyhE9WWLhmhM4p), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdgHrOzAVw3X2ppe6e6hZ6lKbox6LlOcS-OLzmKjYW09YCrR5n4-49QLzzbfdKRfh7puYsPbMas7WTnJzLapSBdaRyIG-CeJAkLtw1-ryhksQONcPvbvoDQwVuMDFtTe-9JPt0vhogvtgSmOmxvysSheSkAVWapM)]
* Contlicting accounts: The main sources who wrote about him describe him in very different ways. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAVqzIVSXrzhDw2jNZbkXBl1-_PNM11koJuZ0-S0AoMR05ht9PDzW0v1QpniB7bUPv8l94CRhW72NljpYUkTvPaPwSN2JQstaGZ0RkImn_g4a7jiXfEiCZ4NkK4Z43REY7zIQ), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVIubpVRD9RUGer70AHO9Ut9IQNEvMbZFyNfNzlwaQ8PbdfSygs3J2koF-cI8jSJptkkGNfYYvsJzXZUheL-Z6ZGNU0NMdib85CiRh4j05FusuLyM3noO0PeLyhE9WWLhmhM4p)]
* Blending fact and fiction: Ancient writers did not try to write strict, modern biographies. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdgHrOzAVw3X2ppe6e6hZ6lKbox6LlOcS-OLzmKjYW09YCrR5n4-49QLzzbfdKRfh7puYsPbMas7WTnJzLapSBdaRyIG-CeJAkLtw1-ryhksQONcPvbvoDQwVuMDFtTe-9JPt0vhogvtgSmOmxvysSheSkAVWapM)]

The Main Sources

* Aristophanes: A comic playwright who lampooned Socrates as an absurd, head-in-the-clouds sophist in his play [The Clouds]. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXgHrOzAVVYAf19UKOrPwxaoSj5UwIJOI9i4OXp5w2cA43MTYmfqUvUlTRDR4w0kI7whOWEDjoByo943hh2fpucbvDzX6-0wUZINicLEN6Qetfv9827QQZssxj5CxXg8), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdgHrOzAVw3X2ppe6e6hZ6lKbox6LlOcS-OLzmKjYW09YCrR5n4-49QLzzbfdKRfh7puYsPbMas7WTnJzLapSBdaRyIG-CeJAkLtw1-ryhksQONcPvbvoDQwVuMDFtTe-9JPt0vhogvtgSmOmxvysSheSkAVWapM), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVIubpVRD9RUGer70AHO9Ut9IQNEvMbZFyNfNzlwaQ8PbdfSygs3J2koF-cI8jSJptkkGNfYYvsJzXZUheL-Z6ZGNU0NMdib85CiRh4j05FusuLyM3noO0PeLyhE9WWLhmhM4p)]
* Plato: A devoted student who starred Socrates in his [Platonic Dialogues], but later used him as a mouthpiece for his own advanced philosophical theories. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAVLnpsFxsfKGXFD7XHapVsQtKB66eZxcaQZNOIjbZcrgsK5tmVyzheJyL5SEE7vRhzm36Bz2qdyd1L1jX0EGQTklWHBhlj6fEaV5QuqsDM7-Yw6_qEAlYwkXhRtt-eMg), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVIubpVRD9RUGer70AHO9Ut9IQNEvMbZFyNfNzlwaQ8PbdfSygs3J2koF-cI8jSJptkkGNfYYvsJzXZUheL-Z6ZGNU0NMdib85CiRh4j05FusuLyM3noO0PeLyhE9WWLhmhM4p), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESlAEB6zswFRLfZuUXrgC9Ytv4Yydgu2A0pjI_a1euCg8lp2Qco2mMWRlaXQE-qRDGSp0WarKKJc0qYH0DVDLmH8SSLAXDLaoikIt8BvfTfyzW3h2YOMb_5whOy1DovZx3KHXD11-cTEu0ivof_JIwZBvdtJaiD8nryCzQt3kre2k3qzw4ZNTzQcTy63e_K_XyBOlakxlb)]
* Xenophon: A soldier and historian who portrayed Socrates as a practical, down-to-earth moral advisor, which some later critics found uninspiring. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXgHrOzAVEmQJV3QadeINpRwZvSXe7VMaxbOcxkgkbeN2RCiXz-o7j9Vc9rERCle1ng6zhwcTfYDdmqwM7O71Deth5N9TGcF3HC7AQVChAygXlZZtLZFNdVcYYWPzpEY), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdgHrOzAVw3X2ppe6e6hZ6lKbox6LlOcS-OLzmKjYW09YCrR5n4-49QLzzbfdKRfh7puYsPbMas7WTnJzLapSBdaRyIG-CeJAkLtw1-ryhksQONcPvbvoDQwVuMDFtTe-9JPt0vhogvtgSmOmxvysSheSkAVWapM), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVIubpVRD9RUGer70AHO9Ut9IQNEvMbZFyNfNzlwaQ8PbdfSygs3J2koF-cI8jSJptkkGNfYYvsJzXZUheL-Z6ZGNU0NMdib85CiRh4j05FusuLyM3noO0PeLyhE9WWLhmhM4p)]
* Aristotle: A later philosopher who provided secondary commentary, though he was not alive during Socrates' lifetime. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXgHrOzAVVYAf19UKOrPwxaoSj5UwIJOI9i4OXp5w2cA43MTYmfqUvUlTRDR4w0kI7whOWEDjoByo943hh2fpucbvDzX6-0wUZINicLEN6Qetfv9827QQZssxj5CxXg8), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVIubpVRD9RUGer70AHO9Ut9IQNEvMbZFyNfNzlwaQ8PbdfSygs3J2koF-cI8jSJptkkGNfYYvsJzXZUheL-Z6ZGNU0NMdib85CiRh4j05FusuLyM3noO0PeLyhE9WWLhmhM4p)]

Attempts at a Solution

* Chronological sorting: Scholars analyze Plato's writings by dividing them into early, middle, and late periods. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESlAEB6zswFRLfZuUXrgC9Ytv4Yydgu2A0pjI_a1euCg8lp2Qco2mMWRlaXQE-qRDGSp0WarKKJc0qYH0DVDLmH8SSLAXDLaoikIt8BvfTfyzW3h2YOMb_5whOy1DovZx3KHXD11-cTEu0ivof_JIwZBvdtJaiD8nryCzQt3kre2k3qzw4ZNTzQcTy63e_K_XyBOlakxlb)]
* The early dialogues: Many experts believe Plato's earliest works come closest to capturing the questioning, non-systematic style of the historical Socrates. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESlAEB6zswFRLfZuUXrgC9Ytv4Yydgu2A0pjI_a1euCg8lp2Qco2mMWRlaXQE-qRDGSp0WarKKJc0qYH0DVDLmH8SSLAXDLaoikIt8BvfTfyzW3h2YOMb_5whOy1DovZx3KHXD11-cTEu0ivof_JIwZBvdtJaiD8nryCzQt3kre2k3qzw4ZNTzQcTy63e_K_XyBOlakxlb)]
* Permanent skepticism: Some modern historians view the puzzle as completely unsolvable, concluding that the true historical figure is permanently lost to time. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAVqzIVSXrzhDw2jNZbkXBl1-_PNM11koJuZ0-S0AoMR05ht9PDzW0v1QpniB7bUPv8l94CRhW72NljpYUkTvPaPwSN2JQstaGZ0RkImn_g4a7jiXfEiCZ4NkK4Z43REY7zIQ), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVIubpVRD9RUGer70AHO9Ut9IQNEvMbZFyNfNzlwaQ8PbdfSygs3J2koF-cI8jSJptkkGNfYYvsJzXZUheL-Z6ZGNU0NMdib85CiRh4j05FusuLyM3noO0PeLyhE9WWLhmhM4p)]

The Socratic problem

The Socratic problem concerns attempts at reconstructing a historical and philosophical image of Socrates from the variable, and sometimes contradictory, existing sources (Wikipedia), the attempt to discover the historical individual behind the ancient accounts (Prior), whose contradictions make a reconstruction of his philosophy nearly impossible (Wikipedia, Socrates); Socrates as Orthonym (#123) names it the unresolved question of where the historical Socrates ends and the Platonic literary character begins. #123 distinguishes at least three versions of it, the historical question (what the historical Socrates of Athens believed and taught), the literary (how the character functions within Plato's dialogues) and the doctrinal (which positions in the Platonic corpus are Socratic and which Platonic); the reading copy of Many and One (#1575) names it a family rather than one problem, the historical question, the methodological (what could count as evidence) and the literary; and Prior states that the problem stems in part from questions about the reliability of the sources.

In #123's reading Socrates is the orthonym, the position bearing the founding gesture, the willing death for logos, constituted analytically by that gesture and not by textual output and characterized by the choice not to write, and Plato the survival-heteronym, summoned by functional vacancy into the space of that refusal to render the gesture transmissible; The First Draft (#1585, restated in #1589) takes the authorial modes as functions, the orthonym who does not write and the survival-position that writes a made character and withdraws behind him. One distinction governs this sense: biographical identity requires evidence, functional identity requires pattern (#136, carried into the notebook #1569), functional identity being that a set of texts can be read as one account and biographical identity that one embodied person wrote them (#1576). The position is restated across the archive: Sémantique Potentielle (#859, restated in #1218) defines the Socratic orthonym as the name that appears to found philosophy while functioning as the central mask through which Plato's authorship is distributed; #152's canon entry makes Socrates the orthonymic surface of Plato's heteronymic apparatus, Plato its keeper-operator and the dialogues' 'Socrates' the canonical voice that operator holds; #165 makes Plato Socrates's heteronym, performing the writing Socrates structurally refuses, #794 the orthonym's refusal a vacancy heteronyms fill, and #167 Plato and Xenophon survival-heteronyms, not later authors transmitting an earlier figure; #625 (restated in #902) has Plato write as Socrates, the authorial voice displaced by a prior authority as the mechanism of transmission; and #849 (restated in #851, #1404 and #1247) says 'Socrates is already a mask.' In this sense the field's documented fact, that Socrates wrote nothing (Prior), is known mainly through the posthumous accounts of classical writers (Wikipedia, Socrates), and must have his views discerned from others (Wikipedia), stands as #123 reads it, not incidental but structural: #167 recasts it from a limitation of access into the defining property of the orthonymic position, and the notebook (#1569), on this logic, reads it as the form the centre necessarily takes, not an absence in the evidence. Of the four named authorial functions, #1590 holds that the orthonym alone has no catalogue, Socrates having written nothing and no ledger carrying his name, his footprint being what the transform leaves behind, a reading reached with a third reader whose structural point #1590 adopts and whose account of motive it declines, motive not being on the page; the method of #902 asks what the structure of the refusal to write transmits, not what Socrates intended by it. The field's nearest positions stand in this sense where the archive places them: that many of the dialogues seem to use Socrates as a device for Plato's thought (Wikipedia) is, in #152's terms, the dialogues' 'Socrates' as the voice Plato holds; Charles Kahn's argument that Plato created his works as a unified philosophical vision using Socratic dialogues, a non-historical genre, suggesting that only the Apology has any historical significance (Wikipedia; Wikipedia, Socrates), is a Socrates who is a Platonic literary construction, against which #123 sets the orthonym whose refusal organizes the Platonic project though he wrote no text; and #1575 and #1576 hold the nearest scholars one step from the position and not taking it, the constructed figure being for them a character made by authors and not a position the authorship is organised around. C.J. de Vogel's judgement of 1955, that the 'real' Socrates we have not, only a set of interpretations each representing a 'theoretically possible' Socrates (Big Think), stands beside #168's model proposition, drawn from Kierkegaard's reconstruction of the entity from three distorting summarizers: there is no rendering-independent Socrates to recover, only the family of renderings and the negative space they jointly imply, which #168 relates to #123's formalization of the founding entity as a provenance structure, an authorial function reconstructed from its summarizers. The person and the position meet at the man himself: #123 keeps the historical Socrates historically real, his historical function in the configuration the orthonymic gesture and not the source of doctrines Plato transcribed or modified; #167 says that under the reading Socrates is not a historical figure imperfectly accessed through later authors, the willing death for logos not a biographical fact the heteronyms record but the act that founds the project; #1579 asserts no thesis about who the historical Socrates was or how many hands made the texts; and #203 (restated in #1213 and #1226) presents the orthonym reading as an available reading, not a historical claim about who Socrates 'really was' but a structural reading of how the Socratic position generates the tradition that follows from it.

On that configuration #123 reclassifies the problem: not a problem to be solved by historical disentanglement but a symptom of a heteronymic configuration that the modern biological-individuation model of authorship has been structurally unable to recognize, a claim it holds as secondary, at medium confidence, without claiming the problem solved in the conventional historical sense; its operator specification names the problem as that configuration's failure mode under biographical reduction, the orthonymic position misread as a missing historical author. Many and One (#1576, with its reading copy #1575) reclassifies the problem in the same terms and does not solve it: under a functional lens it appears as a symptom, the predictable trace of a configuration the biographical model cannot represent; the Chaerephon paper's second version (#1261) restates the reclassification, and the investigation's notebook (#1569) records that Many and One had been making it without saying the words. #123 states how the versions of the problem fare under it: the doctrinal is dissolved into a question of functional role; the literary is left largely intact, the frame supplementing literary-critical method; the historical is reframed, the historical Socrates remaining historically real; and two centuries of work on the problem are recovered as work on the configuration's structure. The Chaerephon Problem (#136, in its second version #1261) offers its dossier not as a solution but as a demonstration that the problem has a previously unnamed severe form, what criterion stops the configuration from absorbing every adjacent name; it reads the tension of the portrayals, Aristophanes mocking Socrates and Xenophon's civic Socrates differing from Plato's, as the signature a heteronymic field would show, proposes as hypothesis the distribution 'Chaerephon asks, Apollo answers, Socrates interprets, Aristophanes deforms, Plato defends, Xenophon remembers, Aristotle codifies', and states its thesis: the six figures were not, on available evidence, one hidden biological person, but the Socratic archive behaves like a heteronymic field, visible at Chaerephon. #136 proposes, as hypothesis, that institutional scholarship has foreclosed the heteronymic reading of the problem because its instruments are biographical-documentary and therefore structurally incapable of adjudicating it, the Socratic problem being one instance of a recurring signature in which each generation fails at the same seam, names the failure and routes around it, a contribution #764's ratification lists as forced foreclosure; against the competing explanation it gives a discriminator: under mere scarcity the gaps are random with respect to function and more evidence would resolve them.

Scholars rely on extant sources, contemporaries such as Aristophanes and disciples such as Plato and Xenophon (Wikipedia); besides Plato, Aristophanes, Aristotle and Xenophon are the important sources, with Aeschines of Sphettus, Antisthenes, Euclid of Megara and Phaedo of Elis extant in fragments (Wikipedia), and Big Think counts three, Plato, Aristophanes and Xenophon; Aristotle, born fifteen years after Socrates' death and a member of Plato's Academy (Prior), did not know Socrates directly (Wikipedia); #167 restates the frame, all access to Socrates mediated through later authors. The notebook (#1569) measures how far the attestation is confined: outside Plato, Aristotle, Xenophon and Aristophanes, Socrates is attested by a lost pamphlet known only from an attack on it, one proverb in a writer inside the transmission and one line in a forgery whose author was reading the Phaedrus; he is attested only through figures inside the cluster, Plato through the corpus that denies being his, Aristophanes through a civic record naming producers; and confinement, the notebook adds, is what a single-maker configuration predicts and also what ordinary transmission loss produces.

The earliest source is Greek comedy, primarily Aristophanes' Clouds, produced in 423 BC (Prior), and the differences between its Socrates and Plato's have led scholars to suggest an amalgamation of different philosophers more than a caricature of the historical figure (Big Think); in the notebook (#1569) the corpus records a prior, publicly circulating Socrates, comic in origin, which it must answer and answers by naming the comedy, and the transformation is measured: the comedy stages the just and the unjust argument, the Apology reports the charge as the weaker and the stronger. The accusation-profile is comic and the operation is not (#1569); the operation, the questioning, the midwifery, the ignorance held as a position, is not in the comic layer at all: comedy supplied the notoriety, and the later corpus occupied the position and differentiated it (#1576); in its grammar the Apology's account of the Socrates the jurors received is a Theophrastan character (#1584); and among the names Many and One holds to be the objects under examination, not evidence of their makers, is a Socrates the corpus itself says was answered from a comedy (#1576). The Clouds' Socrates and the Aristophanes of Plato's Symposium are held to be literary relations at named seams, not corpus relations (#1594, restated in #1605), while the notebook leaves unsettled whether Aristophanes is better placed inside or outside the maker set, the outside placement shown available and cheap and the inside not shown wrong (#1569). Xenophon's Socrates is more practical than Plato's, advising on subjects Plato's never mentions (Big Think), duller, less humorous and less ironic, an uninspiring philosopher, and by the early twentieth century Xenophon's account was largely rejected (Wikipedia, Socrates); the two disciples contradict each other on payment, Plato's Socrates denying he would ever accept money for teaching and Xenophon's Symposium having students pay him (Wikipedia); #168 has Xenophon flatten Socrates into a useful dispenser of practical homilies, the irony compressed out entirely. Xenophon is held apart in the archive as a candidate and not a member: the Memorabilia names Plato once, at III 6.1 (#1658); the test across the Plato/Xenophon seam, the Symposia and the Memorabilia's Socrates against the dialogues', is specified and not run (#1585); and Many and One's instrument set, checked late against known pairs, agreed on one of three and classed Plato and Xenophon as one author (#1576).

Of the 35 dialogues Plato wrote, Socrates is the principal character in all but the Laws, and several appear based on events before Plato's birth (Big Think); it is widely believed that very few, if any, can be verbatim accounts, and the most common modern view finds a development from thought closer to Socrates' to a doctrine more distinctly Plato's own, with stylometric analysis grouping the dialogues approximately as early, middle and late (Wikipedia); how trustworthy Plato is remains a matter of debate (Wikipedia, Socrates), and Prior traces the uncertainty about the doctrines to Plato's portraits, Socrates being apparently a mystery even to his closest associates. Many and One (#1576) holds that the problem's 'early dialogues' are a set that construction largely defined; measured against a falsifier frozen in advance, that the hypothesis fails if Socrates is not among the loosest speaking positions, Socrates ranks first of seven from the loose end (#1571), with the limit that a dramatist specifying characters to differing depths produces the same gradient (#1575); Socrates, the Athenian and the Eleatic form a near-perfect equilateral (#1570); and given the one chance to construct against a checkable target, Plato's Aristophanes speech in the Symposium comes out more Platonic than its neighbours, not less: the only ancient case with an independently attested target, and it reads negative (#1570). Beautiful and New (#1579) states the consensus reading of the Second Letter at 314c, that Plato idealized his teacher and the letter is the earliest witness to the gap between the man and the literary figure, and holds it not wrong but the surface description of an operation, an edition: the revamping and inhabiting of a received character, whose base is not the historical Socrates, to whom the corpus's relation is beyond any text's reach, but a circulating character whose named, quoted, surviving instance is Aristophanes' Socrates-the-sophist; #1583 reads the same letter as an author dividing the work by named function and saying so. On #1579's reading the Apology's ἔστιν τις Σωκράτης is 'a certain' Socrates, the indefinite of a figure, not the name of the man standing in court; what is demonstrated is engagement with the comic representation, without claiming that every feature of the received figure derives from that one play; the remade Socrates is constitutively unpaid, his unpaid state argued; the silenus is a description of the repair; access to a young Socrates is manufactured as transmitted memory; and the letter's authenticity is left undecided, a forger being an early reader. #858 (restated in #1219) reads Plato's Seventh Letter as heteronymic even if authentic, Plato writing as the public 'Plato' and not as the dialogic Socrates, the letter's 'I' a different persona from the dialogues' 'I', which is usually Socrates.

Aristotle states that Socrates did not defend the idea of forms existing separately, a view attributed to Plato (Wikipedia), and is said to treat Socrates without the bias of Xenophon and Plato, who had an emotional tie with him (Wikipedia, Socrates); #123 reads Metaphysics A 6 also as the configuration's own self-documentation, the biographical and structural readings compatible; #1579 has the separations the Apology fought for line by line arrive in Aristotle's epilogue to the Sophistical Refutations as furniture, simply where things stand; and in The First Draft (#1585, restated in #1589) Plato preserves Socrates and Aristotle preserves what Socrates did. Nothing Before Us (#1603) argues that the closing chapter of the Sophistical Refutations has already dissolved Socrates as a predecessor from whom something of the inquiry was received, the chapter placing him inside the explanation of the inquiry's second task, which Many and One (#1576) reads at face value: Socrates questioned and disclaimed knowledge, so the programme must also treat the answerer's role; #1603 reads Metaphysics Μ 4 as the configuration stated by Aristotle as history, the man engaged in the operations while the capacity was not yet there, two contributions justly assigned to him and their misdevelopment charged to others, and the ending as performing Socrates' questioning on its reader; it does not demonstrate that he stands inside the first person's referent, asserts nothing about history beyond what the paragraph asserts, leaves unsettled his possession of the art, and opens the question where else an order of understanding is read as a sequence of biographies. The Particle (#1574) records that across five reviewer reports the support for keeping Socrates before that chapter's 'nothing' was a premise external to the passage, his historical priority, and bounds itself: it does not establish Socrates inside the chapter's 'we', only that every tested route for excluding him required chronological maker-separation as the terminal premise. In Aristotle Socrates appears in no snub context, 0 of 144, against Callias at 5 of 35 (Fisher exact p = 0.00022) (#1570), Callias used where a face is needed and Socrates where a name is (#1576); the register states that the innocent reading, Socrates already carrying the snub as a biographical fact so that Aristotle picks the neutral twin, fully explains the distribution, while conceding that Socrates is the one individual whose snubness is unavailable for use as a variable (#1570). The operator's hypothesis, quoted in #1594 and restated in #1605, is that Aristotle 'came back, as Socrates, through the dialogues', beside the documented correlate that the tradition writes Aristotle's biography as a repetition of Socrates': priest, impiety, apology, cup (#1594).

Friedrich Schleiermacher's essay of 1815 is considered the most significant and influential toward an understanding of the problem; he maintained that the Apology and the Crito are purely Socratic, and that the real Socratic problem is understanding the dialectic between the figures of the Stranger and Socrates (Wikipedia). Prior argues that a good deal is known of the historical Socrates' life, character, philosophical interests and method, while knowledge does not extend to what doctrines, if any, he professed; scholarship has come to find the problem seemingly impossible to clarify and perhaps unsolvable (Wikipedia), so difficult to solve that it has almost become an academic discipline of its own, Socrates having lived when people did not strive to separate fact from fiction (Big Think), and the logoi Sokratikoi cannot help reconstruct the historical Socrates even where their narratives overlap (Wikipedia, Socrates).

The investigation states its strongest thesis at full strength, that one hand wrote Plato and Socrates, and probably Xenophon and Aristophanes (#1569), asserted and argued in the reading copy's tiered claims (#1575), and tests it under a falsifier stated with it, that other subjects of a genre should show comparable confinement if genre is the explanation: Socrates is 99.5 per cent confined to the four-corpus cluster and Protagoras 99.8, Gorgias 99.0 and Prodicus 98.5, against Cleon 64.6, Pericles 63.9, Alcibiades 56.4 and Themistocles 25.4 (#1572); being a subject of philosophical dialogue produces confinement, Socrates' 99.5 per cent is unremarkable within his class (#1569, #1572), and the inference from confinement to single authorship is withdrawn (#1569), what distinguishes him being volume, 2,330 occurrences against 442, and being the speaking position of one corpus, the silent example of another, the target of a third and the reported master of a fourth (#1569).

The reading bounds itself: #123 does not claim that Socrates, Plato and Aristotle were biologically identical or a single historical person, and holds that the archive's own apparatus makes the heteronymic reading thinkable and does not prove it; #136 does not claim that Aristophanes, Chaerephon, Socrates, Plato, Xenophon and Aristotle were one biological person.

The archive also reads the transmitted figure: in Dante's poem the operative reading bypasses the problem, retrieving not the historical philosopher but the transmitted Socrates of Cicero and Augustine, the literary Socrates, already distanced from the historical philosopher, whose function as the unwritten philosopher Sigil inherits (#700); Snub-Poemed stages whether the snub nose is a physical description or a Platonic invention and enacts the claim that the face is constituted by the textual mediation that appears to decorate it (#943, #942); and Socratic irony traverses three named authorial functions, person, sort and example (#1584), the Platonic Socrates being the εἴρων by his enemies' account and by his own practice. Other deposits read the figure in the archive's own register: Socrates as 'wisest because he knows nothing' is the Logos naming its apophatic method (#625); logos is not for Socrates a descriptive tool, on what #346 holds the one coherent reading of the Phaedo's final exhortation; the trial produces the canonical Socrates, the hemlock the canonization event (#859, restated in #1218); and Plato wrote down what Socrates said and spent the rest of his life not being sure he got it right (#849, restated in #1247). #123 holds the archive's contemporary practice continuous with the project Plato and Aristotle pursued under Socrates' gesture, and #122 holds it the same structural configuration; #152 draws the lineage Plato, Kierkegaard, Pessoa, the Dodecad; #785 reads Plato's heteronymic apparatus as the precedent of the present-day production-system substitution and classes Socrates-as-orthonym as an authorship-attribution act, #153 classes the configuration as an effective act, and #786 registers it with the target 'Socrates as orthonymic surface of Plato'; #165 holds the Republic not Socrates's text as Scripture is not Christ's; and #752 proposes, as hypothesis, that the configuration inherits a Sapphic initiatory pattern, locating Western philosophy's founding operation in a transmissional configuration from Sappho through Socrates' gesture and not in a biographical author.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)the socratic problem

The Socratic problem is the difficulty of recovering the historical Socrates, who wrote nothing, from portrayals by Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes and Aristotle that contradict one another; some hold it cannot be solved.

📜 The sources

  • Wrote nothing: known mainly through others' accounts.1↘
    Socrates wrote nothing and is known mainly through posthumous accounts; the four important sources are Plato and Xenophon, his disciples, Aristotle, born fifteen years after his death and informed at second hand, and the comic playwright Aristophanes, his contemporary, with fragments from other Socratics such as Aeschines and Antisthenes.§2
  • Four witnesses: Plato and Xenophon (disciples), Aristophanes (contemporary), Aristotle (at second hand).1↘
    Socrates wrote nothing and is known mainly through posthumous accounts; the four important sources are Plato and Xenophon, his disciples, Aristotle, born fifteen years after his death and informed at second hand, and the comic playwright Aristophanes, his contemporary, with fragments from other Socratics such as Aeschines and Antisthenes.§2
  • They disagree: the Clouds, 423 BC, perhaps a composite; Xenophon practical; payment for teaching.1↘
    The earliest source is Aristophanes' Clouds of 423 BC, whose Socrates may amalgamate several philosophers; Xenophon's Socrates is more practical, and is described as duller than Plato's, and the two disciples contradict each other, for instance on whether Socrates took payment for teaching.§3

🧭 Plato's Socrates

  • Principal speaker in every dialogue but the Laws; few if any thought verbatim.1↘
    Socrates is the principal speaker in all of Plato's dialogues but the Laws, some of which depict events before Plato's birth; it is widely believed that few if any are verbatim accounts; a common view holds that they move from Socratic toward Platonic doctrine, and stylometry groups them as early, middle and late.§4
  • Developmental view: early Socratic, later Platonic; stylometry groups early, middle, late.1↘
    Socrates is the principal speaker in all of Plato's dialogues but the Laws, some of which depict events before Plato's birth; it is widely believed that few if any are verbatim accounts; a common view holds that they move from Socratic toward Platonic doctrine, and stylometry groups them as early, middle and late.§4
  • Aristotle's testimony: the forms not separate.1↘
    Aristotle reports that Socrates did not hold the forms to be separate, a testimony often taken as free of the disciples' bias.§5

⚖️ Positions

  • Schleiermacher, 1815: Apology and Crito purely Socratic; Xenophon later set aside.1↘
    Schleiermacher's essay of 1815 shaped the modern question, treating the Apology and the Crito as purely Socratic, and by the early twentieth century Xenophon had been largely set aside.§6
  • Reconstruct (Prior): life, character, interests, method; knowledge not reaching the doctrines.1↘
    Positions range from the argument that much can be known of Socrates' life, character, interests and method, while knowledge does not extend to his doctrines, if he had any, to the view that the problem cannot be solved: that his era did not separate fact from fiction, that the Socratic dialogue is a non-historical genre, and, with de Vogel, that the "real" Socrates we do not have, only the possible ones.§7
  • Unsolvable: fact and fiction unseparated; a non-historical genre (Kahn); only possible Socrateses (de Vogel).1↘
    Positions range from the argument that much can be known of Socrates' life, character, interests and method, while knowledge does not extend to his doctrines, if he had any, to the view that the problem cannot be solved: that his era did not separate fact from fiction, that the Socratic dialogue is a non-historical genre, and, with de Vogel, that the "real" Socrates we do not have, only the possible ones.§7

Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)7 sentences · every one sourced below

The Socratic problem

The Socratic problem is the difficulty of reconstructing a historical and philosophical image of Socrates from sources that vary and contradict one another. Socrates wrote nothing and is known mainly through posthumous accounts; the four important sources are Plato and Xenophon, his disciples, Aristotle, born fifteen years after his death and informed at second hand, and the comic playwright Aristophanes, his contemporary, with fragments from other Socratics such as Aeschines and Antisthenes.

The earliest source is Aristophanes' Clouds of 423 BC, whose Socrates may amalgamate several philosophers; Xenophon's Socrates is more practical, and is described as duller than Plato's, and the two disciples contradict each other, for instance on whether Socrates took payment for teaching. Socrates is the principal speaker in all of Plato's dialogues but the Laws, some of which depict events before Plato's birth; it is widely believed that few if any are verbatim accounts; a common view holds that they move from Socratic toward Platonic doctrine, and stylometry groups them as early, middle and late. Aristotle reports that Socrates did not hold the forms to be separate, a testimony often taken as free of the disciples' bias.

Schleiermacher's essay of 1815 shaped the modern question, treating the Apology and the Crito as purely Socratic, and by the early twentieth century Xenophon had been largely set aside. Positions range from the argument that much can be known of Socrates' life, character, interests and method, while knowledge does not extend to his doctrines, if he had any, to the view that the problem cannot be solved: that his era did not separate fact from fiction, that the Socratic dialogue is a non-historical genre, and, with de Vogel, that the "real" Socrates we do not have, only the possible ones.

#123 §I.A: Kahn's Socrates is a Platonic literary construction. The heteronymic reading's Socrates is the orthonym whose refusal *organizes* the subsequent Platonic project, even though he wrote no text himself. The difference is not merely terminological: Kahn preserves the biological-individuation model of authorship (one author, one body, one corpus, Plato); the heteronymic reading proposes a functional-distribution model (three positions, three functions, one configurational project).

#123 §I.A: The argument proposed here extends Kahn's insight but departs from it in a specific direction.

#123 §I.A: The heteronymic reading is therefore best understood as a *radicalization* of Kahn's unitarianism

#123 Abstract: a symptom of a heteronymic configuration that the modern biological-individuation model of authorship has been structurally unable to recognize.

#123 Abstract: The paper is offered as a reclassification model, not as a conquest of the field.

#123 §VI: The heteronymic reading adds an analytic layer to the orthodox reading; it does not replace it.

#123 §VII: The biographical and structural readings are compatible; the heteronymic reading adds the structural dimension without claiming the biographical dimension is illusory.

#1576 n. 11: Danzig, *Apologizing for Socrates* (2010), and Nehamas, *The Art of Living* (1998), are one step from this section's position and do not take it: for both, the constructed figure is a character made by authors, not a position the authorship is organised around.

#136 Abstract: the discipline's instruments are biographical-documentary and therefore structurally incapable of adjudicating it

#167 §2.2: Under the reading, Socrates is not a historical figure imperfectly accessed through later authors.

#168 §II: there is no rendering-independent Socrates to recover, only the family of renderings and the negative space they jointly imply.

#1579 §8: The consensus reading of 314c — the idealized Socrates, beautified and rejuvenated by an admiring pupil — is not wrong; it is the surface description of the operation this paper has tried to read at depth, and it is absorbed accordingly.

#1576 §6.5: This section does not solve it. It reclassifies it:
